newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin flays top prosecutor over unsolved crime.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin flays top prosecutor over unsolved crime.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, joining an increasingly heated debate on crime and punishment in Russia, gave his chief prosecutor a humiliating public dressing down on Tuesday for failing to solve several high-profile murders.

Yeltsin, who is expected to announce a major government shake-up this week following a keynote parliamentary address on Thursday, harangued a silent Prosecutor-General Yuri Skuratov for more than a minute in a clip aired on Russian television.

Criticising Skuratov's failure to take part in a television documentary last weekend on the unsolved 1995 murder of top television journalist Vladislav Listyev, Yeltsin angrily told the nation's top attorney to put his house in order.
"When the Prosecutor-General lets go the reins, things can get badly out of control," Yeltsin said.

"Behind the overall figures, which I am well acquainted with, are hidden some prominent murders which the whole of society is seething about," he said. "Despite your repeated assertions that the Listyev case is nearing an end, this and other cases are practically buried. This cannot be allowed."
Crime, much of it involving mafia-style gangs, has risen sharply since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov was promoted to First Deputy Prime Minister last month as part of Yeltsin's latest campaign to crack down on crime, particularly the large-scale economic lawbreaking that the government says is depriving it of valuable resources and billions of dollars in tax revenue.

But many Russians complain big crime seems to go unpunished while penalties for minor offences -- and even for those yet to be convicted of any offence -- can be extremely severe in the country's overcrowed jails and Soviet-era prison camps.
Debate on the subject, stimulated by moves to abolish the death penalty in accordance with undertakings given when Russia joined the Council of Europe a year ago, has heated up recently.
Skuratov himself warned only on Monday that appalling prison conditions could provoke a "social explosion" among inmates.

Of the million or so Russians in prison, over a quarter are still technically innocent and may wait years to be tried. Some 2,000 inmates died of tuberculosis in 1996 -- a death rate from the disease 10 times higher than on the outside.

Justice Minister Valentin Kovalyov told Interfax on Tuesday he had passed to parliament a federal bill suspending the death penalty following an order by Yeltsin on Friday to put into effect Russia's pledge to the Council of Europe.
Kovalyov warned, however, that replacing execution with life imprisonment would mean a costly prison building programme.
It is not known when the State Duma lower house, dominated by the communist opposition, will debate the bill, which is expected to have a hard time in parliament.

Many parliamentarians, as well as the police, argue Russia needs the death penalty to fight rising crime. Indeed, prison conditions are often so bad that is not uncommon even for those condemned to life imprisonment to petition to be shot.
The Kremlin, which allowed several executions after joining the Council of Europe, has observed an informal moratorium on executions since August, leaving some 500 on death row.
Few of these have links to organised crime, officials say.
Russia executes with a single pistol shot to the back of the head, taking prisoners unawares on the way to the exercise yard.
